crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
children.blurb: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing and adapting text, aims, budgets, and supporting materials from earlier grant applications to answer a new funding call.

children.name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
children.blurb: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body sets for how a proposal must look, what it must contain, and how it must be submitted.

children.name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
children.blurb: Budgets and allowable costs in AI research grants cover the direct and indirect expenses that a sponsor will reimburse, from personnel salaries and fringe benefits to equipment, travel, materials, publication fees, and the compute and data storage that AI projects often require.

children.name: Finding Collaborators
children.blurb: Finding collaborators for grant proposals is the work of identifying people, groups, and institutions whose expertise, resources, or access complements a proposed project.

children.name: Predicting Proposal Success
children.blurb: Predicting proposal success is the use of data and models to estimate whether a grant application will be funded, often before or during review.

sections.body: Grant proposals and funding is the part of AI research work that deals with the paperwork and strategy around asking for money. Artificial intelligence is now used to draft sections from a researcher's past papers, check a proposal against a funder's formatting rules, assemble budget tables, suggest possible collaborators, and estimate how a submission might score. These tools read text, extract requirements, compare documents, and rank people or projects by similarity. They do not replace the researcher's judgment about the idea or the funder's mission. The work is practical and document heavy, and it sits between research administration and machine learning. The site's library of 288 research papers can serve as source material for some of these tasks.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are largely solved as engineering problems. Formatting checks, deadline tracking, budget arithmetic, and basic compliance screening can be automated with high reliability when the rules are explicit and machine readable. Finding potential collaborators from publication records is also mature, though the quality depends on the underlying data. What remains hard is judging novelty, fit with a funder's current priorities, and the unwritten preferences of review panels. Predicting proposal success is the least settled area, because review outcomes are noisy, biased, and often decided by small committees. AI can flag risks and patterns, but it cannot promise funding, and it is not a final authority on eligibility or allowable costs.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section follow the life of a proposal from first draft to final prediction. Drafting Proposals from Past Work is the starting point for turning prior publications and notes into new text. Funder Formatting and Compliance covers the rules that vary by agency and program, including page limits, fonts, and required sections. Budgets and Allowable Costs deals with cost categories, institutional rates, and the evidence needed to justify each line. Finding Collaborators helps a researcher identify people with complementary expertise and a record of working together. Predicting Proposal Success looks at models that estimate review outcomes from text and metadata, and it is best read as a critical survey rather than a promise, while a reader would go to the drafting page for reuse, the compliance page for rules, the budget page for numbers, the collaborator page for people, and the prediction page for expectations.
